title: Testing for Reviewer Anchoring in Peer Review: A Randomized Controlled Trial
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether reviewers in academic peer review anchor to their original scores when they are later exposed to new information, such as an author rebuttal. The authors focus on a common peer-review workflow in which reviewers submit an initial review, receive additional evidence, and then revise their scores. They ask whether revised scores remain biased toward the original score, which could help explain why rebuttals often have limited impact on final decisions.

To test this, the authors ran a randomized controlled trial with 108 participants who were PhD students or PhDs in computer science-related fields. Participants acted as reviewers in a mock conference-review setting over Zoom and reviewed the same fabricated paper. The control group saw a paper with an animated GIF showing a strong result, while the experimental group initially saw a frozen frame of that GIF showing a weaker result. After submitting an initial review, the experimental group was told there had been a technical error and was shown the correct animated version, after which they could revise their scores and comments. The study measured overall scores and category scores, especially the Evaluation category, before and after the manipulation.

The manipulation successfully created a perceived quality difference between the initial experimental version and the control version, especially for the Evaluation category. However, when the revised scores from the experimental group were compared with the control scores, the study found no significant evidence of anchoring. The authors conclude that, in this simulated peer-review setting, reviewers did not systematically remain attached to their initial judgments after seeing corrected information. They note that real-world peer review may still differ in important ways, but this experiment provides no direct support for anchoring as an explanation for muted rebuttal effects.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial, but it does not study a K-12 educational intervention or an AI/technology intervention in education. The paper is methodologically strong for its own question, yet it has essentially no direct relevance to the requested education intervention taxonomy.
impact_tier_rationale: The study measures reviewer anchoring in academic peer review, not student, teacher, or school outcomes. It therefore provides no evidence of impact on K-12 educational outcomes or technology-mediated instruction.
